strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated gap in prior attention-steering hallucination mitigation methods: they ignore both the visual attention sink problem and cross-modal fusion balance between visual and query tokens. This is a coherent conceptual contribution.

The proposed 'gaze shift' mechanism (tracking positive changes in visual attention over information-rich query tokens rather than static averaging) is a simple, intuitive, and empirically validated improvement over static saliency maps, supported by both qualitative visualizations (Fig. 1) and a quantitative bounding-box overlap metric (Table 1) showing more than 2x improvement in saliency localization.

Experiments span three models of different architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B) and multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) as well as general capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), with GIFT consistently outperforming greedy decoding and three recent, relevant baselines.

The ablation study (Table 4) isolates the individual contributions of visual attention enhancement and cross-modal balance preservation, providing solid evidence that both components are necessary rather than just claimed.

Computational efficiency is directly benchmarked against baselines (Fig. 6), showing GIFT is substantially cheaper than VAR (11.10x) and Rel-Attn (1.56x) while only slightly more costly than VAF, supporting the paper's claim of practicality.

The paper is transparent about limitations (query-dependency, lack of dynamic decoding-step selection, residual latency overhead) and provides extensive implementation/hyperparameter details in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters (saliency layer, fusion-enhancement layer range, α, β) are tuned using subsets (10%) drawn directly from the POPE and MME evaluation datasets themselves ('pseudo-validation'), and then the method is evaluated on the same benchmarks in the main results tables. This raises a data-leakage concern that could inflate reported gains relative to baselines that may not have been tuned with the same care/access.

It is unclear whether the compared baselines (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn) were re-tuned with comparable rigor (grid search over layers/coefficients) on the same datasets, or run with their default/reported settings; this asymmetry could bias the comparison in GIFT's favor.

Model coverage is limited to three checkpoints from two architecture families (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2-VL), and only one model size is tested for Qwen2-VL; no baselines are compared for Qwen2-VL, weakening claims of generality across architectures. Newer/larger models cited in the introduction (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-4o) are never evaluated.

Several reported gains on general vision-language benchmarks are essentially at parity with greedy decoding (e.g., MME/SEED differences under 1%), which is framed positively as 'no harm' but provides limited evidence of added reasoning value; more decisive stress tests (e.g., harder reasoning benchmarks) are absent.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for most tables (CHAIR, POPE, MME, SEED) despite decoding and evaluation pipelines that could have some run-to-run variability; only MMHal-Bench scoring is averaged over 5 GPT-4.1 runs.

The method still requires an additional prefill pass up to the chosen saliency layer per query, plus per-step attention modification in fusion layers; while shown to be cheap in the tested setting, scalability to longer contexts, multi-turn dialogue, or video inputs is not examined.

The paper does not compare against contrastive-decoding methods (e.g., VCD, OPERA) despite discussing them at length in Related Work, leaving open how GIFT compares to this popular alternative family of hallucination mitigation methods beyond a qualitative efficiency argument.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it clearly articulates two specific gaps in prior inference-time hallucination mitigation methods (visual attention sink and lack of cross-modal fusion balance) and ties the proposed mechanism directly to these gaps.

The 'gaze shift' saliency computation is a reasonably well-motivated and simply implementable modification over naive attention averaging, and the quantitative bounding-box localization comparison (Table 1) and qualitative heatmaps (Fig. 1) provide some direct evidence that it reduces noise from attention-sink regions.

Experiments span multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) and two general vision-language benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), across two model families and sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B), with consistent gains on hallucination metrics.

Ablations isolating the two proposed components (visual-only enhancement vs. joint visual+query enhancement) and a latency comparison against baselines are included, giving some insight into which parts of the method matter and its practical overhead.
weaknesses: The method depends on four hand-tuned, model-specific hyperparameters (saliency layer, fusion-enhancement layer range, alpha, beta), each selected via grid search on small subsets (50 TextVQA examples; 10% of POPE/MME used as a 'pseudo-validation' set). Since these pseudo-validation sets are drawn from the same test distributions used for final evaluation, there is a real risk of overfitting/information leakage that inflates reported gains and raises doubts about fair comparison with baselines that were not tuned this way.

Baselines (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn) are only evaluated on LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B; no baseline comparison is provided for Qwen2-VL 7B, so the claim of consistent superiority 'across VLM architectures' is only partially substantiated — for the newer/stronger architecture the paper only compares against its own greedy baseline.

The headline abstract claim of 'up to 20.7% improvement' refers to a single metric/model combination (CHAIR Cs, LLaVA-1.5 7B) and is not representative of the generally more modest gains seen elsewhere (e.g., POPE improvements are only ~1-3 points, and SEED/MME show essentially no change vs. greedy), which risks over-stating the overall significance of the contribution.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting across multiple runs/seeds is provided for the main results (aside from averaging 5 GPT-4.1 scoring runs for MMHal-Bench), making it hard to assess whether the reported differences, several of which are only 1-3 points, are robust or within noise.

The core hypothesis that VLMs exhibit human-like 'gaze shifts' is a loose analogy rather than a rigorously justified mechanism; the actual operationalization (positive change in attention to visual tokens conditioned on POS-tagged 'information-rich' words) is a fairly ad hoc heuristic whose connection to the stated cognitive motivation is not formally established.

The paper's own limitations section acknowledges heavy dependence on well-formed, specific user queries, and the method's practical reliance on per-model layer/coefficient tuning limits its claimed 'simple yet effective' and broadly applicable framing, since deploying GIFT on a new model architecture would require repeating the full tuning pipeline.

The ablation in Table 4 excludes CHAIR with a somewhat unconvincing justification ('captioning queries lack sufficient specificity'), which is a post hoc rationalization that reduces confidence in the completeness of the ablation evidence for the full benchmark suite used to tout the method's superiority.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies two concrete, well-motivated gaps in prior attention-steering hallucination mitigation work (visual attention sink and lack of cross-modal fusion balance) and supports these claims with targeted empirical analyses (Figure 1 qualitative saliency maps, Figure 2 layer-wise attention shift magnitudes, Figure 4 joint visual/query attention trends, and the quantitative bounding-box saliency evaluation in Table 1).

The proposed 'gaze shift' saliency computation and the dual visual+query attention steering mechanism are simple, lightweight, and conceptually well justified by the preceding analyses rather than being ad hoc.

Experiments span three VLM backbones of different architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B) and three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus two general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), showing consistent improvements over greedy decoding and three recent competitive baselines (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn).

Thorough ablations isolate the contribution of visual-only enhancement vs. recalibration vs. the proposed joint visual-query enhancement (Table 4), and a coefficient sensitivity study (Figure 5/7) demonstrates a sensible trade-off between hallucination reduction and general reasoning performance.
Computational overhead is empirically benchmarked and shown to be substantially lower than two of the three baselines (Figure 6), supporting the practicality claim.
Qualitative examples (Appendix E) and an honest limitations discussion (including query dependency and residual hallucinations) add credibility and transparency.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons against VAF, VAR, and Rel-Attn are only conducted on LLaVA-1.5 models, not on Qwen2-VL, due to lack of official implementations; this limits the strength of the claim that GIFT 'consistently outperforms all baselines' across all tested architectures.

The method requires per-model hyperparameter tuning (saliency layer, fusion-enhancement layer range, α) via grid search on held-out subsets of POPE/MME, and these same benchmarks (albeit different subsets) are later used for final evaluation; this raises some concern about implicit overfitting to benchmark characteristics and about the practical cost/generalizability of applying GIFT to new, untuned models.

Information-rich token selection relies on a POS-tagging heuristic (spaCy), which is language- and tagger-dependent and may not generalize robustly to non-English queries, noisy phrasing, or domains with different linguistic structure; this is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically stress-tested (e.g., no experiments with deliberately vague/ambiguous queries despite this being flagged as a key limitation).

No variance/error bars are reported for most benchmark numbers (CHAIR, POPE, MME, SEED), aside from MMHal-Bench being averaged over 5 GPT-4.1 scoring runs; this makes it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 3.0% POPE improvement) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise.

MMHal-Bench is re-scored with GPT-4.1 instead of the original GPT-4 (since deprecated) and POPE questions are evaluated without the suffixes used by prior work, which, while reasonable for internal consistency, means reported absolute numbers are not strictly comparable to externally published results for the same benchmarks, slightly complicating reproducibility claims.

The paper does not empirically compare against contrastive-decoding-based hallucination mitigation methods, despite discussing them at length in related work, leaving open how GIFT compares to this major alternative family of approaches in both effectiveness and efficiency.

The qualitative failure case (Figure 12) shows GIFT still hallucinates some details (e.g., 'newsroom' setting), but the paper does not deeply analyze what types of hallucinations remain unaddressed or why, limiting insight into the method's boundary conditions.

strengths: Well-motivated core idea: tracking positive 'gaze shift' changes in visual attention over information-rich query tokens, rather than static average attention, is intuitively grounded and quantitatively validated (Table 1 shows >2x improvement in saliency localization over the static baseline using a bounding-box-based metric).

Addresses a real gap in prior attention-steering methods (VAF, VAR) by jointly considering visual attention sink and cross-modal fusion balance (boosting query token attention proportionally alongside visual attention), which is a sensible and non-trivial extension.

Broad experimental coverage across four VLM architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B, Qwen3-VL 8B) and multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus general capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), with additional AMBER/MMBench results in the appendix showing consistent trends.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of visual enhancement vs. cross-modal balance (Inc.V/Cal.V/GIFT), sensitivity analysis for α and enhancement layer range, and comparison of information-rich word extraction strategies (POS tagging vs. LLM-based).

Good practical considerations: latency benchmarking against baselines (1.13x vs up to 11.10x for VAR) demonstrates the method's efficiency, and layer-selection robustness is validated across datasets and random samples (Appendix A).
Honest limitations discussion (query-dependency, static single-snapshot saliency map used throughout decoding, residual overhead) without overselling the contribution.
weaknesses: The method introduces multiple hyperparameters (saliency layer, enhancement layer range, α, β) tuned via grid search on a 10% 'pseudo-validation' subset of POPE/MME; because these are drawn from the same benchmarks used for evaluation, there is some risk that the reported gains partly reflect benchmark-specific tuning rather than fully independent generalization, and the tuning procedure is not tested on held-out unseen benchmarks before evaluation.

Direct baseline comparisons (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn, VCD) are limited to LLaVA-1.5 models only, since these methods lack Qwen implementations; this restricts the strength of the comparative claims on the more recent, and arguably more relevant, Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL models to comparisons against greedy decoding alone.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the main Table 2/3 results (aside from the layer-selection robustness study in Appendix A), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported improvements, some of which (e.g., POPE gains of 0.3-3.0%) are numerically modest.

The saliency map is computed once from a single pre-fill pass and then held fixed throughout the entire decoding process; the paper does not empirically probe whether this static-per-generation map remains accurate for long outputs where relevant regions might shift (the CHAIR generative task uses up to 1024 tokens), which could be a source of unaddressed error, especially given the acknowledged Qwen3-VL/CHAIR discrepancy explained post hoc as a metric artifact rather than validated rigorously.

The core technical contribution is an incremental evolution of existing attention-steering approaches (Yin et al. 2025; Kang et al. 2025) rather than a fundamentally new paradigm; the two-part novelty (gaze-shift saliency computation and query-attention rebalancing) is reasonable but relatively narrow in scope.

The top-50%-heads heuristic used repeatedly (for saliency computation and enhancement-layer/head selection) is inherited from prior work without deeper independent justification or sensitivity analysis specifically for this design choice.

strengths: The core idea of tracking positive 'gaze shifts' in visual attention over information-rich query tokens rather than static averaged attention is intuitive and is empirically validated (Table 1, Figure 1) to produce more concentrated, less noisy saliency maps than the static baseline.

Experiments span four VLM architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B, Qwen3-VL 8B) and multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench, plus AMBER in the appendix), as well as general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench, MMBench), showing the method does not regress general reasoning while reducing hallucination.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations is provided: contribution of visual enhancement vs. fusion balance, sensitivity to α, sensitivity to enhancement layer range, and choice of information-rich word extraction, along with a latency comparison showing GIFT is far cheaper than contrastive-decoding or sink-recalibration baselines.

Appendix includes robustness checks of the peak-layer selection across random seeds and across two very different datasets (TextVQA, MathVista), which is a nice piece of evidence that the chosen layer is a stable model property rather than a cherry-picked dataset artifact.
Qualitative examples (Appendix I) are illustrative and the paper is generally clearly written with explicit formulas for each step of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the method is essentially a refinement of existing attention-steering hallucination mitigation (Yin et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2025a) and attention-sink recalibration (Kang et al. 2025) work, combining an attention-difference-based saliency map with a proportional query-attention rescaling term. The conceptual leap beyond prior art is modest despite the paper's framing as a new mechanism.

The method depends on a large number of hand-tuned, model-specific hyperparameters (saliency-extraction layer, enhancement layer range, α, β), each selected via grid search on subsets of the very evaluation benchmarks (POPE, MME) used for the main results (Appendix D). This raises concerns about overfitting hyperparameters to the test distribution and undermines the claimed 'robustness' and generality of the approach, since a practitioner applying GIFT to a new model/domain would need to repeat this costly tuning procedure.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and asymmetric: VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn, and VCD are only evaluated against LLaVA-1.5 models, while for Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL the paper only reports GIFT vs. greedy decoding. This makes the strongest headline claims (e.g., 'up to 20.7% improvement,' consistent gains 'across VLM architectures') harder to substantiate rigorously, since on the newer/larger backbones there is no evidence GIFT outperforms competing inference-time methods, only that it beats an uninformative baseline.

No variance/uncertainty is reported for the main results in Tables 2, 3, 5, 6 (single run per configuration, except MMHal-Bench, which is averaged over 5 GPT-4.1 calls). Given some reported gains are small (e.g., POPE improvements of 0.3–1.5 points), the lack of multiple seeds or significance testing makes it difficult to assess whether improvements are robust or within noise.

The quantitative saliency-map evaluation (Table 1) is based only on simple existence questions ('Is there a {object} in the image?') with single, unambiguous bounding boxes, which is a narrow setting that may not generalize to the more complex open-ended queries (captioning, counting, relational questions) the method is also applied to.

The explanation for Qwen3-VL's anomalously high CHAIR scores (attributed to CHAIR's string-matching limitations with 'nuanced' detailed captions) is plausible but post-hoc and unverified; it reads as an attempt to explain away an inconvenient result rather than a rigorously investigated finding.

The method retains non-trivial complexity and a 13% latency overhead plus a multi-stage offline tuning pipeline, which somewhat undercuts the paper's 'simple yet effective' positioning, and the practical deployment burden (per-model/per-domain tuning) is non-negligible even though individual inference cost is low.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper precisely identifies two specific gaps in prior attention-steering hallucination mitigation methods (visual attention sink and lack of cross-modal fusion balance) and proposes a mechanism that explicitly targets both.

The 'gaze shift' saliency map construction is intuitive and empirically validated: Table 1 shows a >2x improvement in bounding-box localization score over the 'static gaze' baseline, and Figure 1/7 provide convincing qualitative evidence that the shift-based map better isolates task-relevant regions and adapts to open-ended or abstract queries.

Broad and diverse experimental coverage: four VLM architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B, Qwen3-VL 8B), three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus two general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), with additional validation on AMBER and MMBench in the appendix.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of visual enhancement vs. cross-modal balance (Inc.V/Cal.V/GIFT), sensitivity to the enhancement coefficient α, robustness to enhancement layer range, and comparison of information-rich word extraction strategies (POS tagging vs. LLM-based).
Favorable efficiency profile: GIFT achieves strong hallucination reduction at only 1.13x the latency of greedy decoding, substantially cheaper than contrastive decoding (VCD, 1.99x) and VAR (11.10x).
Reasonable transparency about limitations (query-dependence of the saliency map, residual latency overhead, lack of dynamic step-wise gating) rather than overstating the method's generality.

Reproducibility details are reasonably thorough (precision settings, GPU used, max token settings, hyperparameter values and selection procedure, robustness checks of the peak-layer choice across datasets and random seeds in Appendix A).
weaknesses: Hyperparameters (α, enhancement layers) are tuned on small 10% 'pseudo-validation' subsets drawn directly from the POPE and MME test benchmarks the method is then evaluated on; this raises concerns about benchmark-specific overfitting and an unfair advantage relative to baselines that are not retuned in the same way, which may inflate reported gains.

The anomalous CHAIR result for Qwen3-VL 8B (higher hallucination score despite being the best model on POPE/MMHal-Bench) is explained post-hoc as a metric artifact without rigorous verification (e.g., manual inspection or an alternative hallucination metric), which weakens confidence in this specific claim.

Comparisons with prior attention-steering/contrastive-decoding baselines (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn, VCD) are only available for LLaVA models, since these baselines lack Qwen implementations; this limits the strength of the main comparative claims for the Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL results, where GIFT is only compared to greedy decoding.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs for CHAIR, POPE, or the general-capability benchmarks (only MMHal-Bench's GPT-based scoring is averaged over 5 runs), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (sometimes just 0.1-0.5 points, e.g., POPE gains) are statistically meaningful.

The default information-rich word extraction (POS tagging) is shown in the paper's own ablation to be clearly suboptimal relative to an LLM-based alternative, suggesting the core mechanism's practical effectiveness is sensitive to this design choice, yet the paper still frames POS tagging as the default without fully quantifying the gap's downstream impact across all benchmarks.

The method still occasionally underperforms individual baselines on specific metrics (e.g., POPE F1 for LLaVA-13B is marginally below VAR), which is appropriately reported but tempers the 'consistently outperforms' framing in the abstract/conclusion.

Layer/coefficient selection and the overall pipeline add non-trivial complexity (multiple stages: POS tagging, saliency-layer identification, enhancement-layer selection, two separate scaling coefficients), which may make faithful reproduction and adaptation to new model families more effortful than the 'simple yet effective' framing suggests.
